blindSummary:
The clearest enacted modern local anti-LGBT bylaw in the country: a 2024 municipal public-order regulation (two articles) prescribes oral and written warnings, cessation of activities, social rehabilitation programmes, and administrative fines of one million units of local currency targeting LGBT people. Enforcement is real but contested: a 2026 field study of the regulation's implementation reports supervision, enforcement and guidance by the local public-order force, with customary, religious and women's-council institutions involved, sanctions of suboptimal effectiveness, and rehabilitation hampered because the facilities barely exist; a 2025 study records people swept up in LGBT sweeps/app findings jumping from 56 in 2023 to 272 in 2024, and customary-law actors pushing parallel measures (a boarding-house barcode system, proposed customary-village regulations on social deviance). A neighbouring district finalised a draft bylaw (two articles) on public tranquility containing an explicit LGBT prohibition with administrative fines in the tens of millions of local currency plus mandated 'rehabilitation' (psychosocial counselling, spiritual guidance, resocialisation) for people of same-sex attraction. An international NGO's discrimination mapping covers eight other units in the country (not this unit, whose key bylaws postdate the study), but documents the same regional-autonomy mechanism this unit's bylaws instantiate.

An enacted bylaw with specified sanctions creates visitor-facing risk (detention, forced rehabilitation programmes, fines) that does not exist in most units; the documented apprehension counts show the bylaw environment is actively policed, though no caning or prosecution under these provisions is recorded.

A 2025 study of non-state-actor handling of LGBT cases in this unit: recorded cases rose from 56 people in 2023 to 272 in 2024 (figures from app detections and sweeps); a customary-law community initiated a customary expulsion sanction, proposed customary-village regulations on social deviance, and a barcode registration system for boarding houses; customary sanctions depend on police follow-through.

A March 2026 report: the neighbouring district's regional legislature finalised an anti-LGBT draft bylaw (public-order articles 13-14) containing an explicit prohibition of same-sex behaviour, administrative fines in the tens of millions of local currency, and mandated rehabilitation (psychosocial diagnosis and counselling, spiritual guidance, resocialisation) with local-government clinics; the council acknowledges expected pro-contra backlash.

An international NGO's 'Creeping Criminalisation' mapping (authors omitted; cached copy): maps discriminatory national laws and regional regulations across eight other sub-national units of this country — the reference for this country's regional-bylaw mechanism; this unit's newer regulation postdates the mapping.
